Next 7 Days...

Today will be a fairly quiet day relative to the weather system
that we see move into the region tonight. Through the morning
hours today we will see isolated to scattered showers over the 
high terrain of south-central Montana which could also come with a
stray lightning strike. The afternoon will be mostly dry and 
clear though. There are several impacts/pieces of the puzzle with 
the Friday and Saturday system so will discuss each impact 
independently. 

There are several things to discuss just when it comes to the wind
potential regarding this system. Starting with the Friday AM gap
wind potential, Livingston will likely have a narrow window of a
good setup. As the parent trough advects into the region, we will
see surface pressure falls over the plains near Billings and 
surface pressure rises over YNP and the nearby high terrain. While
there will be some pressure gradient all night, models do not 
depict the gradient really tightening up until just before 
sunrise. There is some discrepancy though regarding just how 
strong this will be. When looking at the proxy IDA-LWT delta-P,
the models are ranging between 6 and 12 mb on the most recent 
model runs. This is resulting in low to medium confidence in just
how strong the winds will be. Additionally, as the cloud cover 
moves in, it may become a little more difficult to develop the 
strong nocturnal inversion necessary for truly strong winds. 

At roughly the same timeframe (Friday around sunrise) we will need
to keep an eye on the Bighorn Mountains and Sheridan, WY. There
are hints at potentially some mountain wave activity, however
there remain several questions. The first is that models are
fairly inconstant with just how strong and/or high the inversion 
will be at the mountain top. This is likely due to disagreements 
in cloud cover through the nighttime hours. This model 
disagreement extends to the lee side subsidence as well. There is 
agreement that there will be some subsidence in a favorable 
setup, but the strength of which varies greatly between models and
runs. The last piece of the puzzle is the mid level winds 
themselves. There is good confidence in a 700mb jet streak that 
moves over the Bighorns right around sunrise Friday. There is 
decent agreement that the maximum wind speeds at the 700mb layer 
will be just south of our CWA into Johnson Co. It looks 
increasingly likely that the area near Story, WY will be the main 
focus for our forecast area. 700mb wind maximum is consistently 
being depicted between 40 to 50kts. While this could be conducive 
to a windy morning, these speeds do not pose a damaging wind 
threat. This will, of course, be monitored as we get closer to 
the event.

The last windy thing to talk about is much simpler, the mix-down 
winds over the plains. As the previously discussed 700mb jet max 
moves eastwards into NE WY and SE MT through the day Friday, this 
will bring windy conditions to SE MT and NE WY midday Friday. 
Even though model soundings are showing very deep mixing Friday, 
as previously discussed, these winds aloft will not be 
particularly strong. The rest of the region will see breezy winds
as well during the event as winds aloft will be in the 30 to 40kt
range with broad-scale subsidence behind the main vort max. While
this will make for a windy day Friday, again, do not foresee any 
highlight worthy gusts at this time. 

Although most of the talk around this system has been centered
around the precipitation and wind, there is also a dry aspect 
that requires attention due to the potential fire weather 
concerns. The main area of concern is Northern Wyoming and far 
Southeast Montana. This is, as previously discussed, the area that
will see the strongest winds during the event. Friday daytime RH 
values are forecast to be the low 20s percent. Although isolated 
values below 20 percent are expected, this will not be 
widespread. The greater concern is just to our SE in northeast WY.
All this to say, elevated fire weather conditions are forecast 
Friday afternoon in these areas. 

The last piece of this puzzle to talk about is the precipitation.
This time last night the QPF totals came up quite significantly,
and tonight it is the opposite. Amounts have come way down across
the entire forecast area. It seems like everyone will see a few 
drops of rain but most to all of the accumulation wil fall to the 
west of Billings. Even the snow totals in the mountains came down 
a lot. The highest forecast snow totals at the peaks of the 
Beartooths right now are 6" at most. The greatest impacts from the
snow will be to anyone recreating in the high country, and those
traveling the Bozeman Pass Friday night. Impacts to travel and 
recreation do not take much snowfall, especially with breezy 
conditions.
